narrativeProgression.description: Introduction of the rotating table and the purpose of the experiment.
Demonstration of the ball rolling straight across the stationary table.
Demonstration of the ball deflecting to the right or left depending on the table's rotation direction and speed.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I'm going to do experiments using our rotating table.
It's about a meter in diameter and I'm going to roll balls down that little ramp.
And when the table is not rotating, the ball travels straight across.
When the table rotates, the camera, which is a fixed in the rotating frame, will see the
Coriolis deflection of the ball.
It deflects off to the right when I move the table in a right-handed sense.
Now by hand, I'm going to move it to the left and you'll see it's going to deflect the
other way.
Now we're going to use the motor on the table to rotate at a constant rate.
And what you'll see is the faster the table rotates, the more Coriolis deflection the ball
feels.
So at 4 RPM, you see the ball deflects a little bit.
Now we'll increase the rotation rate to 8 RPM and the ball will be deflected more.
And it does.
It's deflected about twice as much.
Lastly, at 12 RPM, the ball's deflected even further to the right of its intended path.
In a right-handed system, that's rotating counterclockwise, the deflection of the particle
is off to its right.
Furthermore, we see that the strength of deflection increases with the rapidity of the rotation
of the system.

youtube_description: Laboratory demonstrations of the Coriolis effect.  A ball bearings travels down a ramp that is affixed to rotary table.  The camera in the rotating frame show the ball's deflected path.  We show how deflection varies with direction of rotation and with rotation rate.
